items.title: Ioannidis argued most published research findings are false
items.claim: John Ioannidis's 2005 PLoS Medicine paper made what claim?

options.text: Most published research findings are false — because of low prior probability of true effects, low power, flexibility in analysis, and selective reporting; the title was 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'

items.reveal:
Ioannidis used a Bayesian framework: a positive finding's probability of being true depends on prior probability of the hypothesis, power, type I error rate and bias. For exploratory research with many tested hypotheses and small studies, the probability that a 'significant' result is true can be below 50%.

The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 Science paper directly tested this in psychology: of 100 replications, 36% were significant in the same direction as the original. Effect sizes averaged about half the original. Hardly any of those original findings were obviously wrong; many were inflated by methodological flexibility.
items.why: The replication crisis isn't unique to psychology — it has hit medicine, economics, marketing and machine learning. The methodological response (preregistration, larger samples, registered reports) is reshaping research practice.

items.title: What split-brain patients reveal
items.claim: Roger Sperry's split-brain research (Nobel Prize 1981) studied patients whose corpus callosum had been severed to treat what condition?
items.reveal_title: The surgery was a last-resort epilepsy treatment
items.reveal:
Commissurotomy was performed to prevent seizures from spreading between hemispheres. Sperry and Gazzaniga then used these patients to study hemispheric specialisation in the 1960s and 70s.

The research showed each hemisphere could process information independently when communication was cut.
items.why: Some of the most important findings about the brain came from rare clinical populations.

items.title: What we know about Little Albert
items.claim: John Watson and Rosalie Rayner's 1920 'Little Albert' study conditioned an infant to fear a white rat. What is now believed about the child's identity?

options.text: His identity was always public knowledge
Later researchers proposed identifications but no consensus exists
He grew up to become a famous psychologist
Records confirm he kept the conditioned fear for life

items.reveal:
Beck, Levinson and Irons (2009) proposed Douglas Merritte; Powell et al. (2014) proposed William Barger. The case remains unresolved.

The study itself would not meet modern ethical standards for research with infants.
items.why: Ethical reviews now prevent such studies. Their existence in the historical record shapes how we teach research ethics today.
